title: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
summary: Why BM25 misses documents that use other words, and how stemming, mined synonyms, Rocchio and RM3, doc2query and LLM prompts recover them, measured per query.
outcomes: Explain why vocabulary mismatch caps BM25 recall no matter how k1 and b are tuned
Compute BM25 scores before and after synonym expansion and the resulting precision and recall
Choose index-time or search-time synonyms and predict what a multi-word rule does to an AND query
Mine synonym candidates from reformulations, co-clicks and embeddings, and explain why each needs review
Compute a Rocchio update and trace RM3 pseudo-relevance feedback, including query drift
Run and evaluate Rocchio and RM3 on a test collection, reporting per-query wins and losses
Compare doc2query, learned sparse expansion, query2doc, HyDE and LLM prompts on quality, latency and risk

lessons.title: Vocabulary mismatch: why BM25 misses relevant documents

blocks.md:
BM25 scores a document by summing a weight for every query term the document contains. Recall from the BM25 course: each matched term contributes its IDF times a saturating, length-normalized term-frequency factor. A query term the document does not contain contributes exactly 0.

That is the whole problem this course is about. Manning, Raghavan and Schutze, authors of the textbook *Introduction to Information Retrieval* (2008), call it **synonymy**: the same concept is written with different words, so a search for *aircraft* should also match *plane* (but only the airplane sense, not the woodworking tool). If a relevant document shares no analyzed term with the query, no choice of $k_1$, $b$ or IDF can retrieve it.

Here is a toy collection of 10 short documents, already analyzed (lowercased, stop words such as *the* and *of* removed). The query is `car repair`, and four documents are relevant to it:

- d1 `car repair shop brakes` (relevant)
- d2 `automobile mechanic fix engine brakes` (relevant)
- d3 `vehicle maintenance repair guide` (relevant)
- d4 `car rental airport deals`
- d5 `bicycle repair kit`
- d6 `auto insurance quote drivers`
- d7 `phone screen repair`
- d8 `automobile engine overhaul mechanic` (relevant)
- d9 `auto save document settings`
- d10 `fix software login bug`

blocks.prompt: Score `car repair` with BM25 ($k_1 = 1.2$, $b = 0.75$). Which of the four relevant documents end up with a score of exactly 0, and which irrelevant document ranks second?
blocks.reveal: d2 and d8 score **0**: they say *automobile*, *mechanic* and *fix*, never *car* or *repair*. d3 matches only *repair* and scores 0.40. The second-ranked document is **d4, car rental** (0.67), because *car* is rarer than *repair* and so carries more IDF.

blocks.md: To measure a ranking, this course uses two numbers. **Precision at k** (written P@k) is the fraction of the top k results that are relevant. **Recall at k** (R@k) is the fraction of all relevant documents that appear in the top k. With four relevant documents, a top 3 that holds one of them has precision 1/3 and recall 1/4.

blocks.title: BM25 scores for the query car repair

scenes.caption: Original query, N = 10 documents, average document length (avgdl) 3.9 tokens. Only 5 documents match at all. d1 leads with 1.07; d4 (car rental) is second with 0.67.
Green bars are relevant. Two of the four relevant documents (d2, d8) score 0 and are invisible to every ranking built on these scores.
Precision at 3 is 1/3 (d1, d4, then d5 or d7 tied at 0.45). Recall at 3 is 1/4. Even recall over all 5 matches is only 2/4 = 0.5.

blocks.md: The numbers come straight from the BM25 formula with the IDF of Lucene (the open-source Java search library inside Elasticsearch and OpenSearch), $\ln(1 + (N - n + 0.5)/(n + 0.5))$, where $N$ is the number of documents and $n$ the number that contain the term. *car* appears in 2 of 10 documents (IDF 1.482) and *repair* in 4 (IDF 0.894). Every document here has 3 to 5 tokens, so length normalization barely moves anything. The ranking is fine given the terms it sees; the terms are the problem.

Better scoring cannot fix a zero-overlap miss. Query expansion changes **which documents can match at all** by adding terms to the query (or, in document expansion, to the documents). That is a recall tool first, and every added term is also a new way to match the wrong document.

The safest expansion is one you may already run. A **stemmer** cuts words down to a shared stem so different forms of a word match each other. Elasticsearch's `stemmer` token filter uses the [Porter algorithm](https://snowballstem.org/algorithms/porter/stemmer.html) (Martin Porter's 1980 suffix-stripping rules) for English by default. In the toy corpus the documents say *repair*, so the query `repairs` or `repairing` matches nothing without a stemmer; with Porter all three become `repair` and match d1, d3, d5 and d7.

Because the same analyzer runs on documents at index time and on queries at search time, stemming is expansion applied symmetrically: every form of a word collapses onto one indexed term. It is still a precision bet, as the figure shows.

blocks.title: Stemming collapses word forms onto one indexed term

scenes.caption: Porter stemmer: repairs, repairing and repaired all become repair, so a query in any form matches a document in any form. Recall goes up at no query-time cost.
The same stemmer maps university, universe and universal to one stem, univers. A search for university now matches universe: overstemming, a precision loss.

Porter2 (the Snowball English stemmer, offered as porter2 in Elasticsearch) still merges the repair forms but keeps universiti, univers and universal apart. Stemmer choice is an expansion decision. Computed with PyStemmer.

blocks.md: Manning et al. sort the fixes into two families. **Global methods** expand the query independently of what it retrieves: a thesaurus, a synonym list, WordNet (a hand-built dictionary of English from Princeton that groups words by meaning). **Local methods** look at the documents the query initially retrieves and adjust the query from them: relevance feedback (a person marks which results are relevant) and pseudo-relevance feedback (the system simply assumes the top results are relevant). Two newer families use learned models: expanding *documents* at index time (doc2query) and asking a large language model to write text that is added to the query (query2doc, HyDE).

blocks.title: Where each kind of expansion plugs into a BM25 engine

scenes.caption: Plain BM25: the query is analyzed into terms and looked up in the inverted index.
Global: synonym rules rewrite the analyzed query before lookup (lessons 2 to 4).
Local: take the top-k results, extract terms from them, and run a second, expanded query (lessons 5 and 6).
Model-based: doc2query adds predicted queries to documents before indexing; query2doc and HyDE ask an LLM at query time (lessons 7 and 8).

blocks.question: A colleague proposes fixing the missing d2 and d8 by lowering $b$ so short documents are not favored. What happens?
options: d2 and d8 move up because length normalization was hiding them
Nothing useful: d2 and d8 contain no query term, so every BM25 setting gives them 0
d2 rises but d8 stays at 0 because d8 is shorter
They get matched only if $k_1$ is also raised above 2
blocks.explain: BM25 sums over query terms present in the document. With zero shared terms the sum is empty, whatever $k_1$ and $b$ are. Only changing the terms (expansion) can make them candidates.

blocks.question: Which of these is a *local* method in the Manning et al. sense?
options: A synonym file mapping car to automobile
Looking up each query word in WordNet
Extracting frequent terms from the top 10 results and re-querying with them
Lowercasing and stemming the query
blocks.explain: Local methods adjust the query using the documents it initially retrieves (pseudo-relevance feedback here). Synonym files and WordNet are global: they expand the same way regardless of results. Stemming is ordinary analysis, applied to documents and queries alike.

lessons.title: Synonym expansion on the toy corpus: recall up, precision at risk

blocks.md: The simplest global method is a synonym list. Suppose it says *car* has synonyms *automobile*, *auto* and *vehicle*, and *repair* has synonym *fix*. The expanded query is `car repair automobile auto vehicle fix`, scored with the same BM25 as before: each document gets the sum of the contributions of every expanded term it contains.

blocks.title: BM25 contribution of each expanded term per document

scenes.caption: Only the two original columns count before expansion: d2 and d8 rows are empty there.
Add the synonyms. d2 gains automobile and fix (0.604 each, lower than others because d2 is 5 tokens long); d8 gains automobile.
vehicle appears in only 1 document, so its IDF is 1.992 and it gives d3 0.896, more than car gives d1. Rare synonyms can outweigh the user's own words.
The cost: auto also matches d6 (car insurance, not repair) and d9 (auto save, a different sense), and fix matches d10, a software bug.
Original query: 5 matches, 2 of them relevant.
Expanded, every term at weight 1: all 10 documents now match. Top 3 are d3 1.30, d2 1.21, d1 1.07, all relevant. But d8 (0.67) ties with four irrelevant documents.
Added terms at weight 0.5: original terms dominate again. d1 1.07, d3 0.85, then d4 car rental 0.67 sneaks back to third, ahead of d2 at 0.60.

blocks.md: Manning et al. note that added terms may be weighted less than original query terms. The weight is a dial between trusting the user's words and trusting the synonym list, and the toy numbers show that no single setting wins on every metric.

blocks.title: Precision and recall as the expansion changes

scenes.caption: Original query. P@3 = 0.33, R@3 = 0.25; of the 5 matches, 2 are relevant (0.4) and they cover half the relevant set.
Full synonyms, weight 1. P@3 jumps to 1.0 and every relevant document now matches. But 6 irrelevant documents match too, so precision over all matches stays 0.4.
Weight 0.5. Still full match-level recall, but d4 retakes third place: P@3 = 0.67, R@3 = 0.5.
Weight 1 without the ambiguous synonym auto. d6 and d9 stop matching: 8 matches, 4 relevant (0.5), and the top 3 is unchanged.

blocks.md: Misconception: expansion always helps. It helps when the added words mean the same thing **in this query's context**. *auto* means automobile in d6 but automatic in d9; a list that ignores sense trades recall for false matches. Here the bad synonym cost nothing at the top only because the good documents happened to score higher.

A general-purpose thesaurus makes the sense problem worse. In [WordNet](https://www.nltk.org/howto/wordnet.html), words are grouped into **synsets** (sets of synonyms sharing one meaning). The WordNet guide of NLTK (the Natural Language Toolkit, a Python library) shows `wn.synonyms('car')` returning five senses: `auto, automobile, machine, motorcar`, then `railcar, railroad_car, railway_car`, then `gondola`, `elevator_car` and `cable_car`. Expanding with all senses would send a car repair query toward elevators and cable cars.

Real engines also avoid a second problem: in a plain OR, the rarest synonym gets the biggest IDF, as *vehicle* did above. When single-word synonyms are stacked at the same position (the analyzer emits each synonym at the position of the original word, as lesson 3 shows), Lucene's `QueryBuilder`, the class that turns analyzed query text into a Lucene query, builds a `SynonymQuery`. It scores the group as if it were one indexed term: it sums the term frequencies of all synonyms in the document and uses the **maximum** document frequency (df, the number of documents that contain a term) among them. On the toy corpus d3 drops from 1.30 to 1.07, the same score as d1, because *vehicle* is now weighted like *car*.

blocks.question: You add the rule `car, auto, automobile, vehicle` to a product search. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Precision rises and recall falls, because more terms make the query stricter
Recall rises; precision may fall because auto also appears in contexts like auto save or auto insurance
Nothing changes for ranking, because BM25 ignores terms the user did not type
Both rise with certainty, because all four words mean the same thing
blocks.explain: Expansion is an OR: more terms means more matching documents, so recall can only stay the same or rise. Whether precision suffers depends on how often the synonyms appear in other senses, as d6 and d9 show.

blocks.question: In the toy corpus, why did vehicle contribute 0.896 to d3 while car contributed only 0.666 to d1, both in 4-token documents?
options: vehicle appears in 1 document and car in 2, so vehicle has the higher IDF
Synonyms get an automatic 1.35x boost
d3 is shorter than d1
car is a stop word in this analyzer
blocks.explain: Same length and term frequency, so the difference is IDF: 1.992 for df 1 against 1.482 for df 2. Lucene's SynonymQuery avoids this by using the maximum df of the group.

lessons.title: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch

blocks.md:
Elasticsearch and OpenSearch are search servers built on Lucene; OpenSearch is the open-source fork of Elasticsearch that Amazon started in 2021. Both apply synonyms inside the **analyzer**, the pipeline that turns text into indexed terms: a tokenizer splits the text into tokens, then **token filters** change, remove or add tokens one by one (lowercasing is a token filter). Synonyms are a token filter that adds or replaces tokens. Two filters exist: `synonym` and `synonym_graph`. Rules are usually written in the Solr format, named after Apache Solr, another search server built on Lucene (WordNet format is also supported):

- **Equivalent** rules are comma-separated and interchangeable: `laptop, notebook`.
- **Explicit** rules use `=>` and replace the left side with the right side: `personal computer => pc`.

The `expand` parameter (default `true`) makes every term in an equivalent rule map to every other term, so `foo, bar, baz` gives nine mappings: each of the 3 terms maps to all three terms, itself included, and three times three is nine. With `expand: false`, all of them map to the first term only.

blocks.prompt: With `expand: false`, the rule `car, automobile, auto` is applied at both index and search time. A document says *automobile*; the user types *auto*. Does it match?
blocks.reveal: Yes. With `expand: false` both words are rewritten to the first term, *car*, on both sides, so the document is indexed as *car* and the query becomes *car*. This is **contraction**: one canonical term instead of three, which keeps the index smaller but loses the ability to tell the original words apart.

blocks.md: Multi-word synonyms are where the two filters differ. A token stream records each token's **position**; a token can also span several positions through its `positionLength`. Together these form a **token graph**. Elastic's docs (Elastic is the company behind Elasticsearch) use the example `domain name system is fragile` with the rule that *dns* means *domain name system*.

blocks.title: Token graph for domain name system is fragile

scenes.caption: The original text: five tokens at positions 0 to 4.
synonym_graph adds dns at position 0 with positionLength 3, so it spans the three words. Two valid paths now lead to is fragile.

A match_phrase query (it needs the words next to each other, in order) uses the graph to build two sub-queries, dns is fragile and domain name system is fragile, and a document matching either phrase matches.
The older synonym filter records dns with the default positionLength 1. The graph now claims dns is followed by name: an invalid graph, which the docs warn can give unexpected results.

blocks.md: Indexing ignores `positionLength` entirely, so a graph cannot be stored faithfully in the index. That is why the Elastic docs say `synonym_graph` is designed to be used **as part of a search analyzer only**, and why the plain `synonym` filter, which is required for index-time synonyms, is not recommended when you need multi-word synonyms. OpenSearch documents the same two filters ([synonym_graph](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/analyzers/token-filters/synonym-graph/)).

`match_phrase` is the easy case. A plain `match` query joins its terms with OR by default, and with `operator: and` every term must match. The Elastic docs say that with `synonym_graph` the `match` query turns each multi-word synonym into a phrase query (`auto_generate_synonyms_phrase_query`, default `true`): the rule `ny, new york` gives `(ny OR "new york")`.

We checked what that does to AND by running Lucene's `QueryBuilder` (the class from lesson 2) with a `synonymGraph` filter holding the rule `tv, television, flat screen`, over five product titles indexed without synonyms.

blocks.prompt: Query `flat screen tv mount` with operator AND. Titles: A `wall mount for flat screen tv`, B `television wall mount bracket`, C `flat screen mount`, D `tv mount`, E `flat panel tv stand`. Without the rule only A matches. With it, which titles match?
blocks.reveal:
**A, B, C and D**; only E, which lacks *mount*, is left out. The rule fires on *flat screen* and again on *tv*, so Lucene built three required groups, not four required words:

`+(tv television "flat screen") +(television "flat screen" tv) +mount`

Any alternative satisfies a group, so the two-word title `tv mount` passes both concept groups with one word. AND over the user's words became AND over concepts, which is why expanded queries change recall in ways nobody planned. Check new rules with `_analyze` and a few known queries before trusting AND.

blocks.md: The second reason to prefer search time is operational. Elastic recommends search-time synonyms because the synonym set can change without reindexing. Synonym sets created through the synonyms API (or Kibana, Elastic's web user interface) can only be used at search time, and changing them automatically reloads the analyzers that use them. File-based synonyms must be copied to every node and reloaded; the `updateable: true` setting allows that reload and is only for search analyzers.

blocks.caption: Search-time synonyms as the Elastic guide describes: a synonym_graph filter that references a synonym set (create the set first with PUT _synonyms/product-synonyms), used only in the field's search_analyzer.

blocks.md: Create the synonym set before the index that references it. Elastic's guide warns that an index pointing at a missing set becomes inoperable and must be deleted and re-created, or closed and re-opened.
Use the `_analyze` API on your search analyzer to see exactly which tokens (and positions) a query string produces before trusting a new rule.

blocks.question: Your merchandising team edits the synonym list every week and it includes rules like `tv, television, flat screen`. Which setup fits?
options: synonym filter in the index analyzer, reindex weekly
synonym filter at both index and search time so scores stay consistent
Expand synonyms in application code by duplicating every document
synonym_graph in the search analyzer, backed by a synonym set or an updateable file
blocks.explain: Search time lets the list change without reindexing, and synonym_graph is the filter that handles the multi-word entry flat screen correctly. The index-time synonym filter cannot store multi-position tokens faithfully.

blocks.question: A rule `personal computer => pc` is used at search time. A user types `personal computer`; a document contains only `personal computer`, never `pc`. What happens?
options: It matches, because explicit rules keep both sides
It does not match through the synonym: the query is rewritten to pc, and the document was indexed without that rule
It matches only with expand: false
The analyzer rejects the rule because multi-word left sides are invalid
blocks.explain: An explicit rule replaces the left side with the right side. Applied only at search time, the query becomes pc, which this document does not contain. Use an equivalent rule (personal computer, pc) or include the original on the right side if both should match.

lessons.title: Where synonym rules come from: logs, clicks and embeddings

blocks.md:
The previous two lessons started from a ready-made list: *car* means *automobile*, *tv* means *television*. Somebody has to write that list, and almost all of the precision risk from lesson 2 lives in it. A shop with a million queries a day cannot write rules by hand for every word, so teams mine candidate rules from what users and documents already do, then have people check them.

Three sources are standard: how users rewrite their own queries, which results they click, and which words sit close together in a word embedding. Each finds related words. None of them, on its own, can tell a synonym from a merely related word.

**Query reformulations.** Jones, Rey, Madani and Greiner (Yahoo, WWW 2006) mined pairs of successive queries typed by one user on one day: a user who searches *laptop* and then *notebook computer* is telling you the two are interchangeable, at least for them. One pair proves nothing, so they test whether the second query follows the first more often than chance with a **log-likelihood ratio** (LLR): it compares how likely the counts are if $P(q_2 \mid q_1) = P(q_2 \mid \neg q_1)$ against how likely they are if those two probabilities differ. The statistic is asymptotically chi-squared, so 3.84 is the 95% significance line; with millions of phrases they set the threshold above 100 instead.

blocks.caption: The same statistic written over the 2 x 2 table of query pairs: k11 counts pairs (q1 then q2), k12 pairs that start with q1 but continue elsewhere, k21 pairs that end in q2 from another start, k22 the rest; N is all pairs and k with a dot is a row or column total.

blocks.title: LLR of candidate rewrites in a 12-pair toy log

scenes.caption: 12 toy successive-query pairs: laptop then notebook computer 3 times, then laptop bag once; tv then television twice, then tv mount once; iphone case then iphone charger twice; notebook then spiral notebook twice; one other.
Above the 3.84 line: notebook computer (9.0) and television (6.99) are real synonyms. laptop bag (2.39) and tv mount (3.06) fall below it.

The two highest scores, 10.81, are not synonyms: a charger is a different product and spiral notebook is a narrower query. LLR measures association. Jones et al. list dog to cat among the strongest rewrites of dog.

blocks.md: Jones et al. had people grade rewrites into four classes: precise rewrites (*automobile insurance* to *automotive insurance*), approximate ones that narrow or broaden, possible ones in the same category or a complementary product (*eye-glasses* to *contact lenses*), and clear mismatches. Only the first class is a synonym rule. Their Table 2 shows why grading is needed: the strongest rewrites of *dog* include *dogs* (plural), *cat* (another pet), *dog pictures* (more specific) and *80* (noise).

**The click graph.** Wen, Nie and Zhang (WWW 2001) stated the second source as a principle: if users clicked on the same documents for different queries, then the queries are similar. Write the log as a table of queries by clicked documents and compare rows. A simple score is the **Jaccard overlap** of the clicked sets: shared documents divided by all documents either query clicked. Their example cluster, all leading to one encyclopedia article, was *atomic bomb*, *Nagasaki*, *nuclear bombs*, *Manhattan Project*, *Hiroshima*: closely related queries, not synonyms.

blocks.title: Clicks per query and product (toy shop log)

scenes.caption: Each cell counts clicks on a product after a query. Rows that light up the same columns are synonym candidates.
laptop and notebook computer share both laptops: Jaccard 2 of 3 clicked products, 0.67. A good rule.
notebook clicked mostly paper notebooks, with one laptop click. Jaccard with laptop is 0.25: in this shop notebook means paper, so notebook to laptop would be a bad rule.
iphone case and iphone charger also score 0.67, through the case photo and the bundle kit. Same score as the good pair, yet they are complementary products, not synonyms.

blocks.md: **Embedding neighbours.** A word embedding gives every word a vector, trained so that words used in similar contexts get nearby vectors; **cosine similarity** (the dot product of two vectors scaled to length 1) near 1 means very close. That makes nearest neighbours tempting synonym candidates, and it is exactly the trap: antonyms and competitors appear in the same contexts. We embedded single words with the small public model [all-MiniLM-L6-v2](https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2) (a sentence encoder, used here on one word at a time).

scenes.caption: Synonyms score high: cheap and inexpensive 0.86, buy and purchase 0.87, car and automobile 0.87.
So do opposites: cheap and expensive (0.80) beat cheap and affordable (0.73), and buy and sell reach 0.76. A cosine threshold cannot separate them.
iphone sits nearer smartphone (0.75, a broader term) than android (0.57, a competitor). Neither is a synonym; a rule from either would show the wrong products.

blocks.md: Diaz, Mitra and Craswell (2016) found that where the embedding is trained matters as much as the model. A **global** embedding, trained once on a large general corpus, gave the neighbours *cutting, squeeze, reduce, slash* for *cut*. A **local** embedding, trained only on documents retrieved for a topic about gasoline tax, gave *tax, deficit, vote, budget*. On all three test collections (two TREC newswire sets and a web crawl), expansion with local embeddings beat expansion with global ones, for example NDCG@10 0.563 against at most 0.545 on trec12 (TREC ad hoc newswire). Local means per-query training, so it costs like pseudo-relevance feedback, which lesson 5 covers.

Mined pairs are candidates. Turning them into rules means curation:

- **Direction.** Use an equivalent rule (`laptop, notebook computer`) only when both directions are safe. In a shop that also sells paper, write the one-way explicit rule `laptop => laptop, notebook computer` (lesson 3), so *laptop* expands but *notebook* does not.
- **Ambiguity.** Leave out words with several senses in your catalog (*auto*, *notebook*, *apple*), or scope rules to a field or category.
- **Validation.** Test each batch on judged queries first (nDCG or recall, as in *Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG*), then online with an A/B test. Clicks are biased toward what was ranked high; *Click models and unbiased learning to rank* covers correcting for that.

All three signals measure relatedness, not sameness. Reformulations find narrower and sibling queries, co-clicks find complementary products, embeddings find antonyms and competitors. A human or a judged test set still has to say which candidates mean the same thing.

blocks.question: In the toy click table, iphone case and iphone charger have a co-click Jaccard of 0.67, the same as laptop and notebook computer. Should `iphone case, iphone charger` become a synonym rule?
options: Yes: equal co-click scores mean equally good rules
Yes, but only as an index-time rule so it costs nothing at query time
No: they are complementary products sharing a bundle and a photo; a rule would show chargers to people looking for cases
No: Jaccard is only valid for single-word queries
blocks.explain: Co-clicks show the queries are related, not interchangeable. Jones et al. would grade it a possible rewrite (complementary product), not a precise one. Related-search suggestions are a fine use; synonym expansion is not.

blocks.question: Your shop sells laptops and paper notebooks. Which rule lets laptop searches find items titled notebook computer without sending notebook searches to laptops?
options: `laptop, notebook computer, notebook`
`laptop => laptop, notebook computer`
`notebook => laptop`
`laptop, notebook` with expand: false
blocks.explain: An explicit rule rewrites only its left side, so only the query laptop expands, and keeping laptop on the right side keeps the user's own word. The equivalent rules map in every direction, and contraction with expand: false would rewrite notebook to laptop.

lessons.title: Relevance feedback: Rocchio, pseudo-relevance feedback and RM3

blocks.md: Synonym lists are written in advance. The BM25 course used relevance judgments only to re-weight the query's own terms (the RSJ weight); here feedback also adds new terms. **Relevance feedback** learns the expansion from the results instead: the user marks some retrieved documents relevant or not, and the system builds a better query from them. The classic algorithm is **Rocchio's** (1971), introduced in and popularized by Gerard Salton's SMART system (System for the Mechanical Analysis and Retrieval of Text, built at Cornell), stated in the vector space model where queries and documents are term-weight vectors.

blocks.tex: \vec q_m = \alpha\,\vec q_0 + \beta\,\frac{1}{|D_r|}\sum_{\vec d_j \in D_r}\vec d_j \;-\; \gamma\,\frac{1}{|D_{nr}|}\sum_{\vec d_j \in D_{nr}}\vec d_j
blocks.caption: The new query is alpha times the original query, plus beta times the centroid (the average vector) of the known relevant documents D_r, minus gamma times the centroid of the known nonrelevant ones D_nr. Manning et al. suggest alpha = 1, beta = 0.75, gamma = 0.15, and set negative weights to 0.

blocks.md: Run it on the toy corpus. The user searched `car repair`, looked at the results, and marked d1 and d2 relevant and d4 (car rental) nonrelevant. For clarity the vectors are plain term counts (every count here is 0 or 1), restricted to the nine terms in the figure: d1's *shop* and d4's *deals* are left out to keep it small. Including them would add *shop* at 0.375 and *deals* at -0.15 (clipped to 0).

scenes.caption: Start: the query has weight 1 on car and repair, 0 elsewhere.
Relevant centroid: brakes is in both d1 and d2 (1.0, scaled to 0.75); every other term is in one of the two (0.5, scaled to 0.375).
Nonrelevant d4 contributes car, rental and airport, each scaled by gamma to 0.15.
Sum: car 1 + 0.375 - 0.15 = 1.225; repair 1.375; brakes 0.75; rental and airport go negative (-0.15).
Negative weights are set to 0. 7 of the 9 terms shown stay positive (8 counting d1's shop): it learned automobile, mechanic, engine and fix from d2 without any synonym list.

blocks.md: Now use these weights as per-term boosts on BM25: a boost multiplies that term's BM25 contribution, so *repair* at 1.375 counts 1.375 times as much. This is a simplification, since Rocchio itself ranks by vector similarity. Rescoring the toy corpus this way gives d1 1.87, d2 1.36, d4 0.82, d8 0.75 (counting shop would lift d1 to 2.21 and change no ranks). All four relevant documents now match; d8 was never marked but shares *automobile*, *mechanic* and *engine* with d2. d4 still ranks third because *car* kept most of its weight: gamma is small by design, and Manning et al. note positive feedback is much more valuable than negative.

Those boosts are how a BM25 engine really applies Rocchio. Anserini's `RocchioReranker` takes the top documents of the first search (10 by default), builds each one's term-count vector (dropping terms found in more than 10% of the collection), scales each vector to length 1 (L2 normalization: squared weights sum to 1), averages them, keeps the 10 heaviest terms and scales that centroid back to length 1. It adds the centroid to the length-1 query vector with alpha 1 and beta 0.75 (negative feedback is off unless turned on, and then gamma defaults to 0.15) and sends the result as a Lucene query with one clause per term, boosted by its weight. Each clause's BM25 score is multiplied by its boost and the clauses are summed. RM3, next, is issued the same way and differs only in how it picks and weights terms.

**Pseudo-relevance feedback** (PRF, also called blind feedback) removes the user: run the query, *assume* the top k documents are relevant, and do feedback as usual. Manning et al. note it has been shown to improve performance in the TREC ad hoc task (TREC, the Text REtrieval Conference run by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, NIST, since 1992, sets shared tasks with judged answers; the ad hoc task ranks a fixed document collection for new queries), and warn about **query drift**: for a query about copper mines whose top results are mostly about Chilean mines, the expansion can drift toward documents about Chile.

The PRF method used as a baseline in many papers is **RM3**, from relevance models (Lavrenko and Croft, 2001) as used by UMass (the University of Massachusetts Amherst) at TREC 2004. A **relevance model** is a probability distribution over words, $P(w \mid R)$, that estimates which words the relevant documents $R$ tend to use. The UMass paper estimates it from the top-ranked documents (the formula below is their Equation 2), and RM3 is that estimate mixed back with the original query.

Here is how it is computed. For each feedback document $D$, take the word's share of that document, $P(w \mid D)$ (its count divided by the document's length). Weight it by how well $D$ matches the query, $P(Q \mid D)$: the probability that drawing words from $D$'s word distribution would produce the query's words (the example below uses the document's first-pass retrieval score in its place). Divide that weight by the sum over the feedback set so the weights add to 1, and add up over the documents. Keep the most probable terms, then mix with the original query's own word distribution $P(w \mid Q)$: the final weight is $\lambda$ times the feedback weight plus $1 - \lambda$ times the original one, so the original words keep a share of $1 - \lambda$. Anserini, the open-source research toolkit built on Lucene at the University of Waterloo, ships this as its RM3:

blocks.tex: P(w\mid R) \propto \sum_{D \in R} P(w\mid D)\,\frac{P(Q\mid D)}{\sum_{D'\in R} P(Q\mid D')}, \qquad P'(w) = \lambda\,P(w\mid R) + (1-\lambda)\,P(w\mid Q)
blocks.caption: R is the set of feedback documents, the top fbDocs results; P(w|R) is truncated to the fbTerms most probable terms and renormalized. Anserini's defaults: 10 feedback docs (fbDocs), 10 terms (fbTerms), original query weight 0.5 (so lambda, the feedback share, is 1 - 0.5 = 0.5).

blocks.title: RM3 on the toy corpus (2 feedback docs, 5 terms)

scenes.caption: The first-pass BM25 top 2 are d1 (relevant) and d4 (car rental). PRF assumes both are relevant; nobody checks.
Each term gets P(t|d) x doc score, summed over feedback docs. car is in both docs, so it collects 0.25 x 1.07 + 0.25 x 0.67.
Keep the 5 best terms and normalize to sum 1. Three d4 terms tie at 0.1675; the alphabetical tie-break keeps airport.
Mix 50/50 with the original query. The expanded query now contains airport, a term from the car rental document: query drift.

blocks.md: Simplified from Anserini's `Rm3Reranker`, which weights each feedback document's term distribution by its retrieval score exactly like this, then issues the result as a weighted Lucene query; the real code also first truncates each document's vector and drops terms appearing in more than 10% of documents (a stop-word heuristic skipped here because the toy corpus has only 10 documents). Rescoring the toy corpus: d1 0.56, d4 0.32, d5 and d7 0.155, d3 0.14, d2 0.06. *brakes* pulled d2 back in (a recall gain), but P@3 is still 1/3 and the query now rewards airports.

The evidence below comes from **MS MARCO** (Microsoft MAchine Reading COmprehension), a benchmark of about 8.8 million web passages and real Bing search queries, usually with one passage marked relevant per query; *dev* is its held-out development query set. Its main metric is **MRR@10**, mean reciprocal rank at 10: for each query take 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant passage in the top 10 (0 if there is none), then average over queries. A query whose first relevant passage is at rank 1, 2 or 4 scores 1, 0.5 or 0.25, and papers report the average times 100. **recall@1k** is the share of relevant passages found anywhere in the top 1000.

Feedback is only as good as its top k. When the first-pass top results are relevant, PRF finds words the user never typed; when they are off-topic, it amplifies the error. On MS MARCO dev, the query2doc paper reports BM25 MRR@10 18.4 against 15.8 for BM25 + RM3, while recall@1k rose slightly (85.7 to 86.4). The next lesson measures both methods on a collection you can run on a laptop.

blocks.question: Why does Rocchio usually set gamma much smaller than beta?
options: Nonrelevant documents are rare, so their centroid is unstable
Manning et al. report positive feedback is much more valuable than negative feedback
A large gamma makes the query vector longer, which BM25 penalizes
gamma must equal 1 - beta for the vector to stay normalized
blocks.explain: Relevant documents tend to resemble each other; nonrelevant ones are scattered across many topics, so subtracting their centroid says little. Some systems allow only positive feedback, which is gamma = 0.

blocks.question: RM3 with fbDocs = 10 hurts a query whose first-pass results contain only 1 relevant document in the top 10. What is the most direct fix?
options: Raise fbTerms so more terms dilute the bad ones
Lower the original query weight to 0.1
Use fewer feedback documents or a higher original query weight, or skip PRF when first-pass confidence is low
Switch the first pass from BM25 to TF-IDF
blocks.explain: The expansion terms come from the assumed-relevant documents. With 9 of 10 off-topic, more terms or a lower original weight make drift worse. Fewer feedback docs, more weight on the original query, or not applying PRF to this query limit the damage.

lessons.title: Rocchio and RM3 measured on SciFact

blocks.md: Hand-computed feedback on 10 toy documents shows the mechanism, not whether it pays. To measure it we reuse the SciFact setup from *BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting*: 5,183 scientific abstracts from the BEIR benchmark, queries that are scientific claims, 809 training queries used as a dev set for choosing settings and 300 test queries touched once. Analysis is lowercase, stop words removed, Porter stemming, title and abstract in one field; BM25 uses $k_1 = 1.2$, $b = 0.75$. Metric: nDCG@10, as in that course: each relevant abstract in the top 10 counts less the lower it ranks, scaled so a perfect ranking scores 1. Plain BM25 scores 0.698 on dev and 0.677 on test, the same numbers as in that course.

Both feedback methods are reimplemented in about 40 lines of numpy following Anserini's source: the first BM25 search gives the top documents, feedback terms come from their term-count vectors (terms in more than 10% of documents dropped), and the expanded query is scored as boosted BM25 clauses. The defaults are Anserini's: 10 feedback documents, 10 terms, original query weight 0.5 for RM3; alpha 1, beta 0.75 for Rocchio. One CPU process, about 1 ms per query.

blocks.caption: Abridged from the script we ran. C holds the CSR postings from the BM25 course; prune keeps the k largest weights, l1 rescales to sum 1. rocchio mirrors the Anserini steps in the previous lesson.

blocks.prompt: SciFact has about 1.1 relevant abstracts per query (BEIR's statistics). Before looking: do Anserini's default RM3 and Rocchio raise or lower test nDCG@10 from BM25's 0.677?
blocks.reveal: **Both lower it.** RM3 falls to 0.657 and Rocchio to 0.637. With about one relevant abstract per query, typically 9 of the 10 feedback documents are nonrelevant even when the first search is perfect, so most expansion terms describe neighbouring topics. And a claim is already a long, precise query: there is little vocabulary gap left to close.

scenes.caption: Our numpy run: BM25 0.677, RM3 with Anserini's defaults 0.657 (-0.020, 1.9 paired standard errors: borderline), Rocchio 0.637 (-0.040, 3.3 standard errors). Feedback hurts on average.
Best of 36 RM3 settings on the 809 dev queries: 1 feedback doc, 5 terms, original weight 0.9 (dev 0.701 against 0.698). On test it gives 0.679: +0.002, standard error 0.004, so no measurable gain.
Cross-check with Pyserini on its prebuilt one-field SciFact index (Lucene analyzer, k1 0.9, b 0.4): 0.679, then 0.646 with RM3 and 0.628 with Rocchio, all defaults. Same story from the real engine.

blocks.md: The average hides two kinds of query. On query 1226, *The loss of the TET protein functions may have dire biological consequences, such as myeloid cancers*, BM25 finds no relevant abstract in the top 10. The feedback documents are about TET2 and hematopoiesis, so RM3 adds the stems `tet2`, `tet1` and `hematopoiesi`, and the relevant abstract (on Tet1 and Tet2) rises to rank 3: nDCG@10 goes from 0 to 0.5. On query 1319, *Transplanted human glial cells can differentiate within the host animal*, BM25 has the relevant abstract at rank 2. The top documents include neuron reprogramming papers, RM3 adds `neuron`, `neural`, `brain` and `mhc`, and the relevant abstract drops out of the top 20: 0.63 to 0.

blocks.title: RM3 weights (defaults) for two SciFact queries

scenes.caption: Query 1226: the new terms tet2 (0.099) and tet1 (0.038) name the exact proteins the relevant abstract is about. Expansion closes a real vocabulary gap.
Query 1319: neuron (0.063) and neural (0.057) now outweigh the user's own glial (0.056), pulling in neuron papers. That is query drift on real data.

blocks.md: In a real engine you do not write this yourself. Pyserini, the Python front end to Anserini, exposes both methods on a searcher; the run below is the cross-check in the chart. It needs Java 21 or newer and downloads a prebuilt SciFact index of about 10 MB on first use. The same three calls work on `msmarco-v1-passage`, whose prebuilt index is several gigabytes.

blocks.code:
from pyserini.search.lucene import LuceneSearcher

s = LuceneSearcher.from_prebuilt_index("beir-v1.0.0-scifact.flat")
s.set_bm25(0.9, 0.4)                       # Anserini's BM25 defaults
hits = s.search("0-dimensional biomaterials lack inductive properties", k=10)

s.set_rm3(fb_terms=10, fb_docs=10, original_query_weight=0.5)
hits_rm3 = s.search("0-dimensional biomaterials lack inductive properties", k=10)

s.unset_rm3()
s.set_rocchio(top_fb_terms=10, top_fb_docs=10)   # alpha 1, beta 0.75, gamma 0

# our run over the 300 test claims, nDCG@10:
# bm25 0.6789   + rm3 0.6457   + rocchio 0.6278
blocks.caption: Pyserini's API as installed in our run (set_rm3 and set_rocchio signatures from the library). We scored the hits with the same nDCG@10 function as the numpy run.

blocks.md: Pseudo-relevance feedback is a bet that the first page is mostly relevant. On collections with one relevant document per long, precise query, such as SciFact, the bet loses on average, and tuning on dev only recovers BM25. Measure on your own judged queries before turning it on.

blocks.question: On the dev queries the best RM3 setting used original query weight 0.9 and 1 feedback document. What does that tell you?
options: RM3 is broken in this implementation
SciFact needs more feedback documents, not fewer
A weight of 0.9 means 90% of the query is feedback terms
The tuning found the setting closest to plain BM25: the safest RM3 is the one that changes the query least
blocks.explain: All five best dev settings (within 0.001 of each other) used weight 0.9, with 1 or 10 documents, so the weight is the robust signal: the original query keeps 90% of the mass. When feedback mostly hurts, the optimizer pushes toward no feedback, and the test gain (+0.002 with standard error 0.004) is indistinguishable from zero.

blocks.question: RM3's defaults gave 0.657 against BM25's 0.677 on test, yet 41 of the 300 queries improved. Which conclusion is right?
options: RM3 helps 41 queries and hurts more (54), so a per-query decision could beat both, if you can predict which is which
41 wins means RM3 is better
The 205 unchanged queries prove RM3 does nothing
The loss is noise because the standard error is 0.004
blocks.explain: Means hide per-query effects: 41 wins, 54 losses, 205 ties. Whether you can tell in advance which queries will win is the question of the last lesson. 0.004 is the tuned run's standard error; the default run's is about 0.011, so -0.020 is 1.9 standard errors, borderline at the usual 95% line. The per-query split matters either way.

lessons.title: Expanding with models: doc2query, query2doc and HyDE

blocks.md: Learned models give two more places to add words. **Document expansion** adds them to every document once, at index time. **LLM query expansion** asks a language model to write text about the query at search time. Both attack the same vocabulary gap as synonyms, with very different costs.

**doc2query** (Nogueira, Yang, Lin and Cho, 2019) trains a sequence-to-sequence model (an encoder-decoder network that reads one text and writes another) on (query, relevant passage) pairs to predict which queries a passage would answer. It samples 10 queries per passage with top-k random sampling (each next word is drawn at random from the k most likely words, so the 10 queries differ) and appends them to the passage before indexing with ordinary BM25. On MS MARCO passage dev, MRR@10 rose from 18.4 to 21.5 and recall@1000 from 85.3 to 89.3 (that paper's BM25 run; query2doc's gives 85.7), with BM25 latency going from 50 ms to 90 ms per query (the longer documents cost some search time). About 31% of predicted non-stop words were new to the passage and 69% copied from it: copying re-weights terms that matter, new words add synonyms. **docTTTTTquery** (also written docT5query) replaces the model with T5, Google's Text-To-Text Transfer Transformer, whose five Ts give the name; the query2doc paper lists it at 27.7 MRR@10.

blocks.prompt: We ran the small public checkpoint `doc2query/msmarco-t5-small-v1` (T5 small trained on MS MARCO query and passage pairs) on toy d2, `automobile mechanic fix engine brakes`, sampling 5 queries. Will the predicted queries contain the words *car* or *repair* that d2 lacks?
blocks.reveal:
Yes, in two of five. The model wrote:

- who fix engine brakes
- what mechanic fix engine brake
- what do mechanic fix engine brakes
- what do you do in a car mechanic repair engine
- what to do when a car mechanic repairs

Appended to d2, these give it *car* and *repair* (after stemming), so the query `car repair` now matches d2 with no synonym list. Most other words are copies (*mechanic*, *engine*, *brakes*), which raise the weight of terms d2 already had. Sampling is random, so another run gives other queries.

blocks.md: Does it pay on SciFact? BEIR reports docT5query (T5 base, 40 queries per document) at 0.675 nDCG@10 against 0.665 for BEIR's own BM25 (Anserini, title and text as separate fields, not our one-field 0.677), and above BM25 on 12 of 18 datasets. We expanded all 5,183 abstracts with the small checkpoint ([doc2query/msmarco-t5-small-v1](https://huggingface.co/doc2query/msmarco-t5-small-v1)), 5 sampled queries each (top-k 10, about 14 minutes on 2 CPU threads), and reran the BM25 from the previous lesson: test nDCG@10 went from 0.677 to 0.687 (26 queries up, 20 down; standard error of the difference 0.006, so 1.8 standard errors: suggestive, not significant on 300 queries), and dev from 0.698 to 0.704. Unlike RM3, it gained on both splits, with no query-time cost beyond longer documents. The model is trained on web questions, not scientific claims, and is far smaller than BEIR's, so treat this as a floor, not the method's best.

**Learned sparse retrieval** goes one step further. Instead of appending generated text and letting BM25 count it, a model such as SPLADE (Formal, Piwowarski and Clinchant, 2021) outputs a weight for terms of its whole vocabulary, so a document gets weight on terms it never contains (expansion) and new weights on terms it does (like doc2query's copying), with a sparsity penalty that keeps the vectors small enough for an inverted index. Inference-free variants run the model only on documents; Geng et al. (2024) report client-side latency about 1.1 times BM25's. The mechanism, training and production use are taught in *Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE*.

**query2doc** (Wang, Yang and Wei, 2023) prompts an LLM with the instruction *Write a passage that answers the given query:* plus 4 example pairs, and gets a pseudo-document $d'$. For BM25 the new query concatenates the original query **5 times** with $d'$, because a short query would otherwise be swamped by a long passage. That is the same knob as the synonym weight in lesson 2, set by repetition.

blocks.caption: query2doc's sparse-retrieval query (their Equation 1; sparse means term matching, like BM25): q plus is the query repeated n = 5 times, followed by the pseudo-document d prime. The main results used text-davinci-003, an OpenAI GPT-3.5 model.

blocks.md: HyDE runs on **dense retrieval**, so here it is in one example. An encoder turns any text into a fixed-length vector (384 numbers for the small model all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Search ranks documents by cosine similarity between the query vector and each document vector, from 1 for the same direction down toward 0 for unrelated text, so no word has to match. On the toy corpus, `car repair` against each document gives d3 0.69, d8 0.63, d5 (bicycle repair) 0.55, d1 0.50, d2 0.49, down to d9 (auto save) 0.02. d2 and d8, invisible to BM25, are now retrieved; the bicycle kit sneaks in. How encoders are trained and searched is covered in *Text embeddings and semantic search*.

**HyDE** (Hypothetical Document Embeddings; Gao, Ma, Lin and Callan, 2022) is the dense-retrieval cousin. An instruction-following LLM (InstructGPT, OpenAI's GPT-3 fine-tuned with human feedback to follow written instructions) writes hypothetical documents for the query. An unsupervised encoder (Contriever, trained by contrastive learning on unlabeled text: two spans cut from the same document are pulled close in vector space and spans from other documents pushed apart, so it needs no relevance labels) embeds them, and the average of the embeddings (optionally including the query's own) is the search vector. The generated text may contain false details; the authors argue the encoder acts as a lossy bottleneck that keeps the relevance pattern and drops specifics, and the search itself is grounded in real documents.

The first chart uses the **TREC Deep Learning 2019** track (TREC DL): 43 queries over the MS MARCO passages, with many passages per query judged by NIST assessors on a four-level scale from irrelevant to perfectly relevant. Its metric is **nDCG@10**, normalized discounted cumulative gain at 10. Each of the top 10 results earns a gain from its relevance grade, divided by log base 2 of its rank plus 1: rank 1 counts in full, rank 3 counts half. The sum is the DCG; dividing by the DCG of the best possible ordering gives a number from 0 to 1, reported times 100.

scenes.caption: BM25 51.2 and BM25 + RM3 52.2: classical PRF barely moves nDCG@10 on this benchmark.
docT5query, trained on MS MARCO and paid for once at index time: 64.2.
HyDE, zero-shot dense retrieval with no relevance labels: 61.3. query2doc on plain BM25: 66.2, a 15-point gain with no fine-tuning.

blocks.title: Per-query latency reported by the query2doc paper

scenes.caption: Plain BM25, top 100 on MS MARCO dev, single thread: 16 ms.
The expanded query has many more terms, so the index search alone takes 177 ms, about 11x slower.
Before that, the LLM call took over 2000 ms (the paper notes it depends on server load). Query-time LLM expansion costs seconds, not milliseconds.

blocks.prompt: query2doc avoids one weakness of RM3 by design. Which one?
blocks.reveal: It does not depend on the first-pass results. RM3 expands from the top-k documents, which may be off-topic (the car rental drift in lesson 5, the glial cell query in lesson 6). query2doc expands from the LLM's own knowledge, as the paper notes. The new risk is different: the LLM can write confident but wrong details, and those words get searched too.

blocks.md: Choose by where you can afford the cost. Synonym rules: free at query time, need curation. doc2query: a one-time indexing cost, no query-time model, needs training data from the domain. PRF: a second search per query, risk of drift. query2doc or HyDE: no training and large gains on TREC DL (query2doc was best above, though docT5query still wins on MS MARCO dev, 27.7 against 21.4 MRR@10), but an LLM call per query and generated text you do not control.

These numbers come from specific benchmarks (MS MARCO, TREC DL) and specific models; on SciFact, RM3 lost while our small doc2query gained about a point. Measure on your own queries with judged results before adopting any expansion: a gain on average can still hurt many individual queries, as the next lesson shows.

blocks.question: A shopping site has a 50 ms search budget, a stable catalog, and logs of queries paired with clicked products. Which expansion fits best?
options: query2doc with an LLM on every query
HyDE with Contriever
Pseudo-relevance feedback with 10 docs and 10 terms on every query
doc2query-style document expansion trained on the logged pairs
blocks.explain: Document expansion moves the model cost to indexing, so query latency stays close to plain BM25, and the click logs are exactly the (query, document) pairs it trains on. An LLM call per query alone exceeds 2 seconds in the query2doc measurements; PRF doubles the searches. An inference-free learned sparse model fits for the same reason: its model runs only on documents.

blocks.question: Why does query2doc repeat the query 5 times before appending the pseudo-document for BM25?
options: To keep the original terms from being outweighed by the much longer generated passage
To raise the query's IDF
Because BM25 ignores terms that appear only once in a query
To force the LLM to stay on topic
blocks.explain: BM25 over a long concatenated query is a sum over many terms; without repetition the passage's words dominate. Repeating q is a weight on the original terms, like the 0.5 weight on synonyms or RM3's original query weight.

lessons.title: LLM expansion prompts, and deciding per query whether to expand

blocks.md: Every method in this course changes some queries for the better and some for the worse. Lesson 6 showed it on SciFact: RM3's defaults lost 0.020 nDCG@10 on average, yet improved 41 of 300 queries. If you could tell those 41 apart in advance, you would expand only them. This lesson looks at the per-query picture, tries simple gates, and then turns to prompting an LLM for expansion terms, measured the same way.

blocks.title: Per-query change in nDCG@10, BM25 + RM3 defaults vs BM25

scenes.caption: SciFact test, 300 queries. 205 are unchanged: with about one relevant abstract per query, the top 10 often keeps it at the same rank.
54 queries lose, 28 of them by 0.25 or more (8 by more than half): a relevant abstract pushed down or out of the top 10.
41 queries win, 20 by 0.25 or more. The mean (-0.020) is the difference of two large, opposite groups.

blocks.md: A **gate** decides per query whether to expand, using only what is known before scoring the expanded query. We tried four single-feature gates on the 809 dev queries, each with its threshold tuned there: query length; the first-pass top score; the gap between the first and second score; and the ratio of the top score to the 10th, a sign that one document clearly stands out. Then we applied each to the 300 test queries. None helped: the best dev gate (expand only when the top score is below 8.5) scored 0.670 on test, below plain BM25's 0.677, and the best of the four on test, 0.678 (expand only when the top score is at least 3.9 times the 10th), is +0.001, a tie. The features barely correlate with the gain (Pearson correlation r, where 0 means no linear relation, between -0.01 and 0.08 on dev).

Predicting which queries expansion will help is hard; simple score-based gates tuned on dev did not transfer to test here. Gates that do hold are rules about the query itself: never expand quoted phrases, exact identifiers (part numbers, error codes, SKUs) or field-restricted queries, because there the user's exact string is the point.

Large language models offer a different expansion source. Jagerman, Zhuang, Qin, Wang and Bendersky (Google, 2023) compared eight prompts on BM25, generated with Google's open instruction-tuned models Flan-T5 (60M to 11B parameters) and Flan-UL2 (20B): **Q2D** asks for a passage that answers the query (query2doc's prompt), **Q2E** asks for a list of expansion keywords, and **CoT** (chain of thought) says *Answer the following query: {query} Give the rationale before answering*. Zero-shot (ZS) versions have no examples; /PRF versions add the top 3 retrieved documents to the prompt. As in query2doc, the original query is repeated 5 times before the generated text.

blocks.title: MS MARCO dev with Flan-UL2 20B (Jagerman et al., Table 1)

scenes.caption: nDCG@10 x 100. Classical PRF (Bo1, Bose-Einstein term weighting from the Terrier search toolkit, with its default 3 documents and 10 terms) costs a point: 23.44 to 22.48.
Keyword lists (Q2E 23.52) barely move it; passages (Q2D 23.96) and chain-of-thought (24.85) help a little.
Adding the top 3 retrieved documents to the prompt gives the largest gains: 25.82 for Q2D/PRF and 26.89 for CoT/PRF.

blocks.md:
Two findings matter for deployment. Size: with Flan-T5 models from 60M to 11B parameters, the Q2D prompt needed at least 11B parameters to match the classical Bo1 baseline on recall@1K, and CoT needed 3B. Domain: on BEIR, classical PRF stayed strong on scientific sets such as TREC-COVID and SCIDOCS, where a general LLM may lack domain knowledge, while question-answering sets gained most. On SciFact, recall@1K moved only from 97.17 to 97.57 with any method.

We checked the size effect ourselves with a model about 20 times smaller than 11B, [Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct), on the 300 SciFact test claims (greedy decoding, up to 128 new tokens, 4 s per query on 2 CPU threads).

blocks.title: SciFact test nDCG@10 with a 0.5B model's expansions

scenes.caption: Query repeated 5 times plus the generated text, scored by the same BM25. Q2D/ZS gives 0.687 (44 up, 28 down), CoT 0.689 (42 up, 33 down).

blocks.md:
In our run even the 0.5B model came out slightly ahead: +0.010 for Q2D/ZS and +0.012 for CoT, but each is only 1.2 to 1.4 standard errors (0.008 to 0.009) from zero, so on 300 queries this is no significant gain, just no loss. That is about what doc2query gave, and unlike RM3 it did not hurt on average. The paper's size threshold was about matching classical PRF on MS MARCO recall, a different bar on a different collection, so the two results do not conflict.

The text itself is unreliable. For query 1226 the model expanded TET as *thymidylate synthase*; the SciFact abstracts call it ten-eleven translocation. The correct words around the error (*myeloid*, *bone marrow*) still matched, but the relevant abstract stayed out of the top 10, and query 1319 fell from 0.63 to 0.50 with Q2D. Cost decides the rest: about 4 s per query in our run (2 CPU threads) against about 0.1 ms for our BM25 over 5,183 abstracts.

Expansion is one member of a family of query-side techniques that this course points to rather than repeats:

- Generating several rewrites, retrieving for each and merging with reciprocal rank fusion: *Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result* and *Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)*.
- Rewriting a chat turn into a standalone query, rewrite-retrieve-read, step-back prompting and decomposition: *Query rewriting and decomposition*.
- Running BM25 and dense retrieval together: *Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval*.
- Where all of these sit in a RAG pipeline: *Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures*.

Treat expansion as a per-query risk. Report wins and losses next to the mean, keep the original query in every expanded query (repetition, weights or an original query weight), and switch expansion off for queries whose exact wording is the point.

blocks.question: A support search sends every query through an LLM rewrite. `error E1234 on X200 printer` comes back as `Why does my printer show an error message?`. What breaks, and what guard prevents it?
options: Nothing: the rewrite is more fluent, so BM25 will rank better
BM25 cannot index digits, so the original query never worked either
It dropped E1234 and X200, the matching page's only distinctive terms; keep the original query in the expanded one and skip expansion for queries with codes or model numbers
The LLM should have expanded E1234 into synonyms such as E1235
blocks.explain: Identifiers are rare terms with high IDF and exactly what the relevant page contains. A rewrite that drops them replaces precise evidence with generic words. Repeating the original query (as query2doc does) keeps them, and a rule that skips expansion when the query contains codes avoids the risk entirely.

blocks.question: Jagerman et al. found the Q2D prompt needed an 11B model to match classical PRF on MS MARCO recall@1K. You can only serve a 1B model. Which plan follows from their results?
options: Prefer a chain-of-thought or PRF-augmented prompt, which held up better at smaller sizes, and measure per-query wins and losses on your own judged queries
Use Q2D anyway; prompt style does not matter at small sizes
Drop the original query so the model's text dominates
Use the zero-shot Q2D prompt, which was strongest in Table 1
blocks.explain: CoT reached parity at 3B, and the paper reports that adding PRF documents stabilizes small models (CoT/PRF beat the other prompts at 770M). Q2D/ZS was the weakest Flan-UL2 prompt (19.54 nDCG@10). Either way, measure on your own data.
